newsitem.title: FRANCE: Eurotunnel reaches outline debt deal with banks.
newsitem.headline: Eurotunnel reaches outline debt deal with banks.

text.p: Eurotunnel, which operates the Channel Tunnel between England and France, reached an outline agreement with six bank lenders on Tuesday to restructure debt and interest totalling some 70 billion francs ($14 billion).
A source familiar with the marathon talks told Reuters: "There has been a global agreement, the details are being finalised this evening."
A spokeswoman for heavily indebted Eurotunnel declined comment. But banking sources in London confirmed an outline pact had been reached.

Talks between Eurotunnel co-chairmen Alastair Morton and Patrick Ponsolle and the creditor banks dragged on into Tuesday evening as they worked on details of the debt refinancing which is vital for the company's future.

Eurotunnel, which operates the rail tunnel opened in 1994, froze payments to 225 banks on part of its debt in September 1995, unable to bear the loans piled up on its balance sheet and cost overruns incurred digging the Franco-British link.
The company has been seeking an agreement on the pricing of an expected debt-for-equity swap and the issue of convertible bonds which would lighten the debt service.

Eurotunnel's Ponsolle and Morton have tried to protect shareholders from a massive dilution of the share capital while the banks, who rank above them as secured lenders, have sought to get as much of the equity as possible in the debt conversion.
Stockmarket analysts in London said Eurotunnel needs to cut out around half of the debt mountain if it is to survive.
"There is one billion pounds of equity, nine billion pounds of debt and 480 million pounds of revenue," said analyst Richard Hannah of investment bank UBS.

French President Jacques Chirac voiced his confidence in the Channel Tunnel while on a visit to the Pas-de-Calais region in the north of France. "The future is positive. I believe, little by little, we will see this machinery becoming more profitable," he told reporters.

The stakes in the negotiations were raised by Eurotunnel in February when it asked the court president, Jean-Pierre Mattei, to name Jean-Pierre Badinter and Lord Wakeham as mediators. That mediation mission ended on Monday and was not renewed.

The court move infuriated the banks, which saw it as the first legal step that could lead to a loss of control and a court-driven solution, with the implicit threat of an insolvency ruling by the court president if they did not accept.

Shareholders, at least 600,000 of them in France, have seen at least two-thirds of their investment drain away since they invested in the 1987 flotation at 35 francs per share. The company also issued new shares in 1994 at 24 francs.
Banks have received millions in fees and interest payments.
Eurotunnel has been a commercial success, winning a 40 percent share of the market in the Dover-Calais route. But it is bowed under by its debt service burden.
Meanwhile, Eurotunnel's share are suspended until the outcome of the talks. The shares closed on Friday at 9.20 francs per share in Paris and 113.5 pence in London.
"There is simply not enough value in the company to satisfy everyone," said a corporate debt specialist.

For the six negotiating banks, they have to be able to "sell" any agreement to the rest of the lending syndicate and argue that this is the best possible deal under the circumstances. All the banks need to consent to the package.
And shareholders must ratify any deal struck with the banks.
